paper_metadata.title: Effects of Hf and Re on the microstructure and mechanical properties of Nb1.6Mo0.3C0.04 alloy

evidence.quote: Carbide-strengthened Nb – Mo-based refractory alloys with nominal compositions of Nb1.6Mo0.3C0.04, Nb1.6Mo0.3C0.04Hf0.04, Nb1.6Mo0.3C0.04Re0.04, and Nb1.6Mo0.3C0.04Hf0.04Re0.04 were fabricated to elucidate the roles of Hf and Re in microstructure evolution and compressive properties.

other.flipping: flipped by 180 degrees between successive melts

evidence.quote: The chamber was evacuated to 5 × 10-4 Pa before backfilling with argon as a protective atmosphere. Arc melting was carried out under a high-purity Ar atmosphere at a current of 400 – 450 A. To improve chemical homogeneity within the ingots, electromagnetic stirring was applied during melting, and each ingot was re-melted five times, with the button ingot flipped by 180° between successive melts.

evidence.quote: The chamber was evacuated to 5 × 10-4 Pa before backfilling with argon as a protective atmosphere. Arc melting was carried out under a high-purity Ar atmosphere at a current of 400 – 450 A. To improve chemical homogeneity within the ingots, electromagnetic stirring was applied during melting, and each ingot was re-melted five times, with the button ingot flipped by 180° between successive melts.
the primary phase in all four alloys was identified as the BCC phase
with a minor amount of FCC phase also present. The lattice parameters of the BCC and FCC phases for these alloys are summarized in Table 1.
the primary phase in all four alloys was identified as the BCC phase
confirming that the precipitates are FCC-structured carbides. In addition, the precipitates are semi-coherent with the BCC matrix.
the #1 alloy exhibits the coarsest grains, with an average grain size of 298.33 μm
an average precipitate length of 27.23 μm. The platelet-like carbides are homogeneously dispersed in the matrix.
the #3-Re alloy shows significant grain refinement to an average size of 178.82 μm
the precipitates remain uniformly distributed with a comparable average length of 22.34 μm
the addition of Hf alone leads to pronounced microstructural refinement, with the average grain size reduced to 127.570 μm
the precipitate length markedly decreased to 2.940 μm. In this case, the carbides exhibit a mixed distribution characterized by the coexistence of clustered and dispersed platelet-like precipitates.
When Hf and Re are added simultaneously (#4-HfRe), both the grain size (130.130 μm)
and precipitate length (3.585 μm) are comparable to those of the Hf-containing alloy, and a similar mixed distribution of carbides is observed.
The #1 alloy exhibits a yield strength of 604.29 MPa.
The #1 alloy has a yield strength of 181.23 MPa and an ultimate compressive strength of 381.60 MPa.

Re provides strong solid-solution strengthening and can increase the recrystallization temperature of the BCC matrix, which benefits both room-temperature and high-temperature strength
